title: Brønsted-Lowry Acids and Bases
lead: In the Brønsted-Lowry view an acid gives up a proton and a base takes one, and each leaves behind a conjugate partner. Water can play either part, toward other species and toward itself, and an equilibrium constant of its own measures how far it ionizes.
objectives: Identify acids, bases, and conjugate acid-base pairs according to the Brønsted-Lowry definition
Write equations for acid and base ionization reactions
Use the ion-product constant for water to calculate hydronium and hydroxide ion concentrations
Describe the acid-base behavior of amphiprotic substances
summary_html:
A compound that can donate a proton (a hydrogen ion) to another compound is called a Brønsted-Lowry acid. The compound that accepts the proton is called a Brønsted-Lowry base. The species remaining after a Brønsted-Lowry acid has lost a proton is the conjugate base of the acid. The species formed when a Brønsted-Lowry base gains a proton is the conjugate acid of the base. Thus, an acid-base reaction occurs when a proton is transferred from an acid to a base, with formation of the conjugate base of the reactant acid and formation of the conjugate acid of the reactant base. Amphiprotic species can act as both proton donors and proton acceptors. Water is the most important amphiprotic species. It can form both the hydronium ion, H3O+, and the hydroxide ion, OH− when it undergoes autoionization:

$${\text{2H}}_{2}\text{O(}l)\;\rightleftharpoons \;{\text{H}}_{3}{\text{O}}^{+}(aq)+{\text{OH}}^{-}(aq)$$

The ion product of water, $\kKw$ is the equilibrium constant for the autoionization reaction:

$$\kKw=\kconcHyd\kconcOH=1.0\;\times \;1{0}^{-14}\;\text{at}\;25\;{}^{\circ}\text{C}$$

exercises.prompt: The ion product of water at 80 °C is 2.4 × 10<sup>−13</sup>. What are the concentrations of hydronium and hydroxide ions in pure water at 80 °C?

answer.hint: In pure water the two concentrations are equal, so K<sub>w</sub> is the square of either one.

exercises.prompt: What is the hydronium ion concentration in an aqueous solution with a hydroxide ion concentration of 0.001 M at 25 °C?

answer.hint: Divide K<sub>w</sub> at 25 °C by the hydroxide ion concentration.

exercises.prompt:
Write separate equations representing the reaction of ${\text{H}}_{2}{\text{PO}}_{4}{}^{-}$
(a) as a base with HBr
(b) as an acid with OH−
Write equations that show NH<sub>3</sub> as both a conjugate acid and a conjugate base.

answer.solution: One example for NH<sub>3</sub> as a conjugate acid: ${\text{NH}}_{2}{}^{-}+{\text{H}}^{+}\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{NH}}_{3};$ as a conjugate base: ${\text{NH}}_{4}{}^{+}(aq)+{\text{OH}}^{-}(aq)\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{NH}}_{3}(aq)+{\text{H}}_{2}\text{O}(l)$

exercises.prompt: Write equations that show ${\text{H}}_{2}{\text{PO}}_{4}{}^{-}$ acting both as an acid and as a base.

answer.solution: As an acid, H2PO4− gives a proton to hydroxide ion: H2PO4−(aq) + OH−(aq) ⇌ HPO42−(aq) + H2O(l). As a base, it takes a proton from hydronium ion: H2PO4−(aq) + H3O+(aq) ⇌ H3PO4(aq) + H2O(l). Losing one H+ leaves its conjugate base, HPO42−, with one hydrogen fewer and a charge one lower; gaining one H+ gives its conjugate acid, H3PO4, with one hydrogen more and no charge. Both equations balance in atoms and in charge, and together they show the ion is amphiprotic.

exercises.prompt:
Show by suitable net ionic equations that each of the following species can act as a Brønsted-Lowry acid:
(a) ${\text{H}}_{3}{\text{O}}^{+}$
(b) HCl
(c) NH3
(d) CH3CO2H
(e) ${\text{NH}}_{4}{}^{+}$
(f) ${\text{HSO}}_{4}{}^{-}$

Show by suitable net ionic equations that each of the following species can act as a Brønsted-Lowry acid:
(a) HNO3
(b) ${\text{PH}}_{4}{}^{+}$
(c) H2S
(d) CH3CH2COOH
(e) ${\text{H}}_{2}{\text{PO}}_{4}{}^{-}$
(f) HS−

answer.solution: Each species donates one proton to water, leaving a conjugate base with one hydrogen fewer and a charge one lower. (a) HNO3(aq) + H2O(l) ⟶ H3O+(aq) + NO3−(aq); (b) PH4+(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ H3O+(aq) + PH3(aq); (c) H2S(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ H3O+(aq) + HS−(aq); (d) CH3CH2COOH(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ H3O+(aq) + CH3CH2COO−(aq), the proton coming from the O–H of the carboxyl group; (e) H2PO4−(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ H3O+(aq) + HPO42−(aq); (f) HS−(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ H3O+(aq) + S2−(aq). In every equation the species gives up an H+, which is what makes it a Brønsted-Lowry acid, and hydrogen atoms and charges balance on both sides.

exercises.prompt:
Show by suitable net ionic equations that each of the following species can act as a Brønsted-Lowry base:
(a) H2O
(b) OH−
(c) NH3
(d) CN−
(e) S2−
(f) ${\text{H}}_{2}{\text{PO}}_{4}{}^{-}$

Show by suitable net ionic equations that each of the following species can act as a Brønsted-Lowry base:
(a) HS−
(b) ${\text{PO}}_{4}{}^{3-}$
(c) ${\text{NH}}_{2}{}^{-}$
(d) C2H5OH
(e) O2−
(f) ${\text{H}}_{2}{\text{PO}}_{4}{}^{-}$

answer.solution: Each species accepts one proton, becoming a conjugate acid with one hydrogen more and a charge one higher. (a) HS−(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ H2S(aq) + OH−(aq); (b) PO43−(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ HPO42−(aq) + OH−(aq); (c) NH2−(aq) + H2O(l) ⟶ NH3(aq) + OH−(aq); (d) C2H5OH(aq) + H3O+(aq) ⇌ C2H5OH2+(aq) + H2O(l), the proton bonding to a lone pair on the oxygen atom; (e) O2−(aq) + H2O(l) ⟶ OH−(aq) + OH−(aq); (f) H2PO4−(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ H3PO4(aq) + OH−(aq). In every equation the species takes an H+ from the acid beside it, which is what makes it a Brønsted-Lowry base, and atoms and charges balance.

exercises.prompt:
What is the conjugate acid of each of the following? What is the conjugate base of each?
(a) OH−
(b) H2O
(c) ${\text{HCO}}_{3}{}^{-}$
(d) NH3
(e) ${\text{HSO}}_{4}{}^{-}$
(f) H2O2
(g) HS−
(h) ${\text{H}}_{5}{\text{N}}_{2}{}^{+}$

What is the conjugate acid of each of the following? What is the conjugate base of each?
(a) H2S
(b) ${\text{H}}_{2}{\text{PO}}_{4}{}^{-}$
(c) PH3
(d) HS−
(e) ${\text{HSO}}_{3}{}^{-}$
(f) ${\text{H}}_{3}{\text{O}}_{2}{}^{+}$
(g) H4N2
(h) CH3OH

answer.solution: Conjugate acid first, then conjugate base: (a) H<sub>3</sub>S<sup>+</sup>, HS<sup>−</sup>; (b) H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>, HPO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>; (c) PH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>, PH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>; (d) H<sub>2</sub>S, S<sup>2−</sup>; (e) H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>3</sub>, SO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup>; (f) H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>2</sub><sup>2+</sup>, H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>; (g) H<sub>5</sub>N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>, H<sub>3</sub>N<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>; (h) CH<sub>3</sub>OH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>, CH<sub>3</sub>O<sup>−</sup>. The two members of a conjugate pair differ by a single hydrogen ion, so the conjugate acid is the species with one H<sup>+</sup> added, one more hydrogen and a charge one higher, and the conjugate base is the species with one H<sup>+</sup> removed, one hydrogen fewer and a charge one lower. For H<sub>3</sub>O<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>, for example, adding H<sup>+</sup> gives H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>2</sub><sup>2+</sup> and removing it gives neutral H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>.

exercises.prompt:
Identify and label the Brønsted-Lowry acid, its conjugate base, the Brønsted-Lowry base, and its conjugate acid in each of the following equations:
(a) ${\text{HNO}}_{3}+{\text{H}}_{2}\text{O}\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{H}}_{3}{\text{O}}^{+}+{\text{NO}}_{3}{}^{-}$
(b) ${\text{CN}}^{-}+{\text{H}}_{2}\text{O}\;\longrightarrow \;\text{HCN}+{\text{OH}}^{-}$
(c) ${\text{H}}_{2}{\text{SO}}_{4}+{\text{Cl}}^{-}\;\longrightarrow \;\text{HCl}+{\text{HSO}}_{4}{}^{-}$
(d) ${\text{HSO}}_{4}{}^{-}+{\text{OH}}^{-}\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{SO}}_{4}{}^{2-}+{\text{H}}_{2}\text{O}$
(e) ${\text{O}}^{2-}+{\text{H}}_{2}\text{O}\;\longrightarrow \;2{\text{OH}}^{-}$
(f) ${[\text{Cu}{({\text{H}}_{2}\text{O})}_{3}(\text{OH})]}^{+}+{[\text{Al}{({\text{H}}_{2}\text{O})}_{6}]}^{3+}\;\longrightarrow \;{[\text{Cu}{({\text{H}}_{2}\text{O})}_{4}]}^{2+}+{[\text{Al}{({\text{H}}_{2}\text{O})}_{5}(\text{OH})]}^{2+}$
(g) ${\text{H}}_{2}\text{S}+{\text{NH}}_{2}{}^{-}\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{HS}}^{-}+{\text{NH}}_{3}$

answer.solution: The labels are Brønsted-Lowry acid = BA; its conjugate base = CB; Brønsted-Lowry base = BB; its conjugate acid = CA. (a) HNO<sub>3</sub>(BA), H<sub>2</sub>O(BB), H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>(CA), ${\text{NO}}_{3}{}^{-}(\text{CB});$ (b) CN<sup>−</sup>(BB), H<sub>2</sub>O(BA), HCN(CA), OH<sup>−</sup>(CB); (c) H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>(BA), Cl<sup>−</sup>(BB), HCl(CA), ${\text{HSO}}_{4}{}^{-}(\text{CB});$ (d) ${\text{HSO}}_{4}{}^{-}(\text{BA}),$ OH<sup>−</sup>(BB), ${\text{SO}}_{4}{}^{2-}$(CB), H<sub>2</sub>O(CA); (e) O<sup>2−</sup>(BB), H<sub>2</sub>O(BA) OH<sup>−</sup>(CB and CA); (f) [Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>3</sub>(OH)]<sup>+</sup>(BB), [Al(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>(BA), [Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>(CA), [Al(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>(OH)]<sup>2+</sup>(CB); (g) H<sub>2</sub>S(BA), ${\text{NH}}_{2}{}^{-}(\text{BB}),$ HS<sup>−</sup>(CB), NH<sub>3</sub>(CA)

exercises.prompt:
Identify and label the Brønsted-Lowry acid, its conjugate base, the Brønsted-Lowry base, and its conjugate acid in each of the following equations:
(a) ${\text{NO}}_{2}{}^{-}+{\text{H}}_{2}\text{O}\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{HNO}}_{2}+{\text{OH}}^{-}$
(b) $\text{HBr}+{\text{H}}_{2}\text{O}\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{H}}_{3}{\text{O}}^{+}+{\text{Br}}^{-}$
(c) ${\text{HS}}^{-}+{\text{H}}_{2}\text{O}\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{H}}_{2}\text{S}+{\text{OH}}^{-}$
(d) ${\text{H}}_{2}{\text{PO}}_{4}{}^{-}+{\text{OH}}^{-}\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{HPO}}_{4}{}^{2-}+{\text{H}}_{2}\text{O}$
(e) ${\text{H}}_{2}{\text{PO}}_{4}{}^{-}+\text{HCl}\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{H}}_{3}{\text{PO}}_{4}+{\text{Cl}}^{-}$
(f) ${[\text{Fe}{({\text{H}}_{2}\text{O})}_{5}(\text{OH})]}^{2+}+{[\text{Al}{({\text{H}}_{2}\text{O})}_{6}]}^{3+}\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{[Fe}{({\text{H}}_{2}\text{O})}_{6}]}^{3+}+{[\text{Al}{({\text{H}}_{2}\text{O})}_{5}(\text{OH})]}^{2+}$
(g) ${\text{CH}}_{3}\text{OH}+{\text{H}}^{-}\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{CH}}_{3}{\text{O}}^{-}+{\text{H}}_{2}$

answer.solution: The labels are Brønsted-Lowry acid = BA; its conjugate base = CB; Brønsted-Lowry base = BB; its conjugate acid = CA. (a) NO<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>(BB), H<sub>2</sub>O(BA), HNO<sub>2</sub>(CA), OH<sup>−</sup>(CB); (b) HBr(BA), H<sub>2</sub>O(BB), H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>(CA), Br<sup>−</sup>(CB); (c) HS<sup>−</sup>(BB), H<sub>2</sub>O(BA), H<sub>2</sub>S(CA), OH<sup>−</sup>(CB); (d) H<sub>2</sub>PO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>(BA), OH<sup>−</sup>(BB), HPO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>(CB), H<sub>2</sub>O(CA); (e) H<sub>2</sub>PO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>(BB), HCl(BA), H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>(CA), Cl<sup>−</sup>(CB); (f) [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>(OH)]<sup>2+</sup>(BB), [Al(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>(BA), [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>(CA), [Al(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>(OH)]<sup>2+</sup>(CB); (g) CH<sub>3</sub>OH(BA), H<sup>−</sup>(BB), CH<sub>3</sub>O<sup>−</sup>(CB), H<sub>2</sub>(CA). In each equation the acid is the reactant that loses one H<sup>+</sup>, and the product with one hydrogen fewer is its conjugate base; the base is the reactant that gains that H<sup>+</sup>, and the product with one hydrogen more is its conjugate acid.

exercises.prompt: What are amphiprotic species? Illustrate with suitable equations.

answer.solution: Amphiprotic species may either gain or lose a proton in a chemical reaction, thus acting as a base or an acid. An example is H<sub>2</sub>O. As an acid: ${\text{H}}_{2}\text{O}(aq)+{\text{NH}}_{3}(aq)\;\rightleftharpoons \;{\text{NH}}_{4}{}^{+}(aq)+{\text{OH}}^{-}(aq).$ As a base: ${\text{H}}_{2}\text{O}(aq)+\text{HCl}(aq)\;\rightleftharpoons \;{\text{H}}_{3}{\text{O}}^{+}(aq)+{\text{Cl}}^{-}(aq)$

exercises.prompt:
State which of the following species are amphiprotic and write chemical equations illustrating the amphiprotic character of these species:
(a) H2O
(b) ${\text{HPO}}_{4}{}^{2-}$
(c) S2−
(d) ${\text{CO}}_{3}{}^{2-}$
(e) ${\text{HSO}}_{4}{}^{-}$

answer.solution: H2O, HPO42− and HSO4− are amphiprotic; S2− and CO32− are not, because they have no hydrogen to donate and can act only as bases. (a) As an acid: H2O(l) + NH3(aq) ⇌ NH4+(aq) + OH−(aq); as a base: H2O(l) + HCl(aq) ⟶ H3O+(aq) + Cl−(aq). (b) As an acid: HPO42−(aq) + OH−(aq) ⇌ PO43−(aq) + H2O(l); as a base: HPO42−(aq) + H3O+(aq) ⇌ H2PO4−(aq) + H2O(l). (e) As an acid: HSO4−(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ H3O+(aq) + SO42−(aq); as a base, toward an acid stronger than sulfuric acid: HSO4− + HClO4 ⟶ H2SO4 + ClO4−. Each amphiprotic species carries a hydrogen it can lose and a lone pair that can take on a proton.

exercises.prompt:
State which of the following species are amphiprotic and write chemical equations illustrating the amphiprotic character of these species.
(a) ${\text{NH}}_{3}$
(b) ${\text{HPO}}_{4}{}^{2-}$
(c) Br−
(d) ${\text{NH}}_{4}{}^{+}$
(e) ${\text{AsO}}_{4}{}^{3-}$
Is the self-ionization of water endothermic or exothermic? The ionization constant for water (Kw) is 2.9 × 10−14 at 40 °C and 9.3 × 10−14 at 60 °C.

answer.solution: The self-ionization of water is endothermic. As the temperature rises from 40 °C to 60 °C, Kw rises from 2.9 × 10−14 to 9.3 × 10−14, so at the higher temperature the equilibrium 2H2O(l) ⇌ H3O+(aq) + OH−(aq) lies further to the right and more water is ionized. By Le Châtelier’s principle, raising the temperature shifts an equilibrium in the direction that absorbs heat. Since heating shifts this one toward the ions, the forward reaction absorbs heat, and its enthalpy change is positive.
